Joanne: Oh, you do the crossword? The proper one?
Alison: The cryptic, yes. Badly. My husband says I only do it so I can complain about the setter.
Joanne: I do word searches. They're more my level, if that makes sense. I do them on my break at work.
Alison: What do you do?
Joanne: I'm a domestic at the hospital. On the wards, cleaning. I've been there eleven years now. I'm on earlies, so I'm up at half five, which is why I look like this, sorry.
Alison: You look fine. Half five is brutal though. Which hospital?
Joanne: The general in Basingstoke. I've lived there all my life, really. I've never gone more than about five miles, Gary says.
Alison: There's a lot to be said for that. I'm in Tonbridge. I work for the council, planning, so I spend all day reading about people wanting to put extensions where they shouldn't.
Joanne: Oh, that sounds very clever. I'd worry about getting it wrong.
Alison: It's mostly reading. And sitting in meetings while people shout at you. You sort of learn not to take it personally. I imagine you get a bit of that too.
Joanne: Not shouting, really. The patients are mostly lovely. The elderly ones especially, they get frightened, you know, and you just have a little chat while you're doing round their bed. Some of them know me by name. Sorry, I'm going on.
Alison: No, you're not. That's the bit that actually matters, isn't it? The talking.
Joanne: I think so. The nurses haven't always got time, so. Erm, have you got a dog? I saw a lead in your picture.
Alison: Well spotted. Biscuit. Labrador cross, very elderly and very lazy. He won't go out if it's raining, he just stands in the doorway and looks at me.
Joanne: No! My cat's called Biscuit.
Alison: Is it really?
Joanne: She's nineteen. She's getting a bit doddery now, she sort of walks into the table leg.
Alison: That's quite a coincidence. Two elderly Biscuits. Perhaps it's a South East thing.
Joanne: My daughter named her. Kirsty. She was about ten. She's twenty-nine now and she's got a little boy, he's just started saying Nanny Jo.
Alison: Oh, that's lovely. Mine are thirty-two and twenty-nine, no grandchildren yet. I'm not holding my breath. My daughter's in south London, so I get the train up and we have lunch and she tells me what I'm doing wrong.
Joanne: Kirsty does that. Mostly about my phone.
Alison: Mine taught me "tbh". I'm not sure I've thanked her for it.
Joanne: My son's in Reading now. Liam. He moved last year for work. I text him more than I should, probably.
Alison: I don't think there's a should with that. They'd tell you if it was too much. Well, mine would. Bluntly.
Joanne: That's true. I just, I don't know, I miss him, you know. The house is quiet.
Alison: It is quiet. You get used to it. Sort of. Graham fills it with DIY he never finishes.
Joanne: Gary's the same. There's a shelf in the hall that's been —
Alison: Since spring?
Joanne: Since Christmas!
Alison: Oh, you're winning. We've got a timer going, I think we're nearly —

Leanne: Hiya. Right, last one. Leanne.
Alison: Alison. Hello. You've got the cat on the filing cabinet.
Leanne: Moth. She's there now actually, judging me. You've got a dog, haven't you? Everyone's been on about Biscuit.
Alison: Apparently he's famous. He's asleep under the table, which is all he does.
Leanne: Where are you, then?
Alison: Tonbridge. Kent.
Leanne: Stockport. Not Manchester. Don't say it.
Alison: I wasn't going to. I did geography at Sheffield, I'm aware there's more than one place up there.
Leanne: Ha, fair. What do you do?
Alison: Planning, at the council.
Leanne: Oh God. Right, so are you the people who let shop signs happen? Because I'm a graphic designer and the high street near me looks like someone sneezed a font catalogue at it.
Alison: Mostly no. Advertisement consent covers size and illumination, not taste. If it's not flashing at drivers, we can't refuse it for being ugly.
Leanne: That's a scandal, that. There should be a font officer.
Alison: I'd apply. I'd turn down the meetings, though.
Leanne: You'd be good at it. You've got a face that says no.
Alison: I've been told. It's useful at committee. People shout and I sort of just wait until they've finished.
Leanne: See, I'd shout back. I told a client last week his logo looked like a 2009 Facebook page.
Alison: Did he change it?
Leanne: He asked for someone else.
Alison: That's usually how it goes.
Leanne: Yeah, well. I'd rather be doing my own prints anyway. Screen prints, zines. I used to skate roller derby, Moth to a Flame, but I've got rheumatoid arthritis now so it's swimming and printing.
Alison: That's a good name. Annoying, the arthritis, I'd imagine. More than annoying.
Leanne: It's a pain. Literally. Some days I can't open a jar. Gavin has to do it and he's dead smug about it.
Alison: Graham does that with the crossword. Puts in the one I couldn't get and doesn't say anything. Which is worse.
Leanne: Oh, the silent ones are worse. Do you read, then? You look like a reader.
Alison: Crime, mostly. Several at once. I don't finish half of them.
Leanne: I do true crime podcasts. Same thing really, just with more adverts. Where do you go on holiday? Let me guess, cottage.
Alison: Pembrokeshire. Northumberland. You've got me.
Leanne: I knew it. I'm city breaks. Berlin, Lisbon, Bologna. Flea markets and galleries.
Alison: I'd go to Bologna. For the arcades. My husband teases me for looking at street layouts.
Leanne: That's actually quite cool. Don't tell anyone I said that. I thought you'd be a bit mardy from your photo.
Alison: I am a bit. I just keep it quiet. Anyway, I should think about dinner after this.
Leanne: Tea. It's tea.
Alison: It's dinner, I'm afraid. I'm from Kent, I'm not —
calls.C0412:
Alison: Hello. Jodie, is it?
Jodie: Yeah, hiya. Sorry, I'm a bit frazzled, that's my fifth. Erm, you're Alison? With Biscuit?
Alison: The very same. He's had more mentions today than he's had walks this week.
Jodie: Ha. Everyone's on about him. Do you know what this pays, by the way? I've asked literally everyone.
Alison: I think it's a voucher. Forty pounds? I didn't read it properly, which is very me.
Jodie: Forty's alright. That's a week of chippy teas. So what do you do? I don't think anyone's said.
Alison: Planning, at the council. In Tonbridge.
Jodie: Oh, so like, extensions and that?
Alison: Extensions, housing estates, the odd furious letter about a fence. Leanne wanted me to ban ugly shop signs, I had to disappoint her.
Jodie: Ha, she would. I used to make them. Banners and signs, at a print firm in Wednesbury. Three years. Did anyone ever need permission for a banner?
Alison: Technically, sometimes. In practice, nobody asks and we don't chase them unless someone complains.
Jodie: That's so much less exciting than I wanted it to be. Erm, I left anyway. I'm doing an MA now, in UX design, in Birmingham. Apps and websites.
Alison: Is that going well?
Jodie: Erm. Honestly? I've had two extensions already and it's only March. I do everything the night before. And sometimes I think, like, I had a proper job, and I've packed it in and got a loan, and what if there's no jobs at the end of it? Sorry, that's a lot. Does that make sense?
Alison: It makes perfect sense. My daughter did something similar at about your age. Left a perfectly decent job, went back to study, panicked for a year.
Jodie: And was it alright?
Alison: She's fine. Better than fine. She still panics, but now she gets paid for it.
Jodie: Ha. That's the dream. You kind of remind me of my mum, by the way. Not in a bad way.
Alison: I'll take it. You've got a look of my daughter, actually. The clip. She wears her hair like that.
Jodie: Does she tell you what you're doing wrong?
Alison: Constantly. Mostly my phone and my inbox. She's not wrong about the inbox.
Jodie: My mum's on the family WhatsApp all day. It never stops. My nan sends voice notes, like, four minutes long, about the weather.
Alison: That's quite a skill, four minutes on weather.
Jodie: She's got stamina. Sunday dinner at hers is the same. She doesn't stop talking or feeding you.
Alison: That sounds rather nice, to be honest.
Jodie: It is, yeah. They just don't really get what I do. I'm the arty one, so I'm, like, "on the computer."
Alison: My family think I spend all day saying no to conservatories. Which isn't entirely untrue.
Jodie: Ha. Are you doing anything nice after this?
Alison: Walking Biscuit, if it's not raining. Then dinner. Something out of the fridge, no recipe.
Jodie: That's my nightmare, no recipe. I can do a chilli and fajitas and that's it.
Alison: That's two more than some people. Oh, that'll be the —
calls.C0413:
Leanne: Hiya. So I told the last one it was my last one. Turns out I can't count.
Joanne: Oh, hello. Sorry, I'm Joanne. I think this is the last one, isn't it? I'm not sure.
Leanne: It's definitely the last one. Probably. Leanne. Stockport.
Joanne: Basingstoke. I clean on the wards, at the hospital.
Leanne: Right. Early starts?
Joanne: Half five. I'm a bit shattered, sorry, if I'm quiet.
Leanne: You're fine. I'm loud enough for both of us, apparently. I'm a graphic designer. Menus, shop signs, that kind of thing. And my own prints.
Joanne: Oh, I saw them on your wall. I wouldn't know what to say about them, sorry. I'm not very arty.
Leanne: You don't have to say anything about them. Most people who do say the wrong thing anyway. Do you like them or not?
Joanne: Erm, I liked the blue one. With the bird.
Leanne: That's a heron. That's the one that sold out. So you've got taste, actually.
Joanne: Oh. Well. I don't know about that.
Leanne: Take it, I don't say it much. Do you get much hydro at your hospital? I do hydrotherapy, I've got rheumatoid arthritis.
Joanne: We've got a hydro pool, yes. I don't do that bit, but I clean near it sometimes. The physios are lovely. Sorry, that must be hard, the arthritis.
Leanne: Some days. I used to skate roller derby. Now I do slow lengths with pensioners. Who are faster than me, which is humbling.
Joanne: My mum's seventy-eight. She had a fall last winter. I worry about her all the time, if I'm honest.
Leanne: Does she live on her own?
Joanne: Yes. She won't move. She says she's fine. I ring her every night and she says I'm fussing.
Leanne: Mine rings me every Sunday at tea time. Without fail. Middle of eating, every time.
Joanne: That's nice, though. That she rings.
Leanne: Yeah. It is, I suppose. Don't tell her I said that.
Joanne: I won't. Sorry, is that a crayon drawing behind you? No, sorry, that's mine. On my fridge. I thought it was your screen for a second.
Leanne: Ha. Who did it?
Joanne: My grandson. He's two. It's meant to be Biscuit, the cat. It looks like a potato.
Leanne: Honestly, that's better than half the logos I get sent. Clients would pay for that.
Joanne: Oh, stop it. He'd be chuffed, though.
Leanne: I'm serious. Bold line, no faff. He's got more confidence than most designers.
Joanne: I'll tell Kirsty. She'll laugh.
Leanne: You're not what I expected, you know. I thought you'd be —

C0407.line_text: Tendai: Ha, slowly. That's fair. I do kitchen extensions, first fix, and the amount of times the builder says "planning's fine, planning's fine," and then it's not fine. Then everybody's waiting, and I've got jobs booked back to back, so the whole week goes out the window. That's my fault, really, I book too tight. Natalie tells me.
C0407.what: A teenage boy in a school jumper walks across the kitchen behind Tendai, opens the fridge, takes out a carton of juice, drinks from it standing with the door open, then puts it back and walks out of frame. Tendai doesn't turn round and carries on talking.
